---
title: "Week 15: The Evidence-to-Power Pipeline"
---

## Theme: Ethics, Community Ownership, and the Future of Public Health
Data Science

Who benefits when community data is published? Who controls it?
Community Benefits Agreements, data sovereignty frameworks, and
Indigenous data rights raise fundamental questions about the ethics of
research-for-policy. We also reflect on the semester\'s arc and discuss
where the field is heading: federated learning, synthetic data, and the
risks and opportunities of large language models in population health
surveillance.

## Classroom Lab Demonstration

**Legal Focus:** Community Benefits Agreements as legally binding
contracts between municipalities/developers and community organizations;
data sovereignty frameworks and Indigenous data rights (CARE
Principles); IRB ethics and community-engaged research standards; FERPA,
HIPAA, and the limits of de-identification.

**Health Focus:** The evidence-to-power gap: why rigorous data often
fails to change policy; community-engaged research as an alternative
model; the future of public health data science --- federated learning,
synthetic data generation, and large language models as population
health surveillance tools.

**Data:** Synthesis and curation of the semester\'s lab work; GitHub
repository as a professional portfolio artifact; peer portfolio audit
checklist (provided on Carmen).

**R Code:** rmarkdown::render() with clean environment to test
reproducibility; usethis::use_readme_md() and usethis::use_github() for
portfolio finalization; git commit and push from RStudio Git pane; final
review of all code annotations and inline comments.

- Conduct structured peer audit of a classmate\'s GitHub portfolio using
  provided checklist rubric

- Finalize GitHub repository structure: README.md, data/, analysis/ (3
  curated labs), policy-memo/, reflection/

- Polish all R Markdown reports --- ensure code is annotated, outputs
  are labeled, and each document knits cleanly from a fresh session

- Write 400-word self-reflection: What did data show that policy missed?
